strengths: The paper addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, π³) accept only raw images, ignoring readily available geometric priors such as calibrated intrinsics, camera poses, and depth measurements. The multi-modal prior prompting mechanism is a sensible and clean solution.

The evaluation is broad and mostly convincing: SOTA results across point map reconstruction (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU), camera pose estimation, surface normal estimation (ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1), and novel view synthesis, with clear gains over VGGT, π³, StableNormal, GeoWizard, and AnySplat. The claimed gains on point map accuracy (10.4%/17.8% mean accuracy) are substantial.

The prior-injection ablations (Fig. 6, Tab. 5) are informative: they show that a single prior modality improves not only its corresponding task but also other tasks, and that compact single-token embeddings outperform dense Plücker raymap encodings — a non-obvious and practically useful finding.

The dynamic prior injection scheme (randomly toggling priors with probability 0.5 during training) is a simple and effective way to support arbitrary prior subsets at inference, and the ablations validate the GS head design and dual context/target supervision.
The limitations section is honest, identifying dynamic/autonomous driving under-representation, resolution limits (300–700 px), and scalability constraints on consumer GPUs.
Additional results (post-optimization initialization, monocular/video depth) demonstrate the model is useful beyond its core benchmarks, e.g., as a strong initializer for per-scene 3DGS optimization.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is limited. The model is built directly on VGGT (explicitly initialized from VGGT pretrained weights) with added modality tokens, DPT heads for normals and Gaussians, and curriculum training. The core contribution is an engineering integration of prior conditioning into an existing architecture rather than a new method or insight, which may reduce its appeal as a main-track contribution.

A potential technical concern is under-examined: depth priors are normalized to [0,1] before tokenization, which discards absolute scale. This seems to conflict with the motivating claim that 'depth measurements ground predictions in areas where image-based cues are alone insufficient' and that calibrated intrinsics/depth resolve scale ambiguity. The paper does not explain how metric depth information survives this normalization, nor how the model distinguishes normalized depth distributions across scenes.

Some results are marginal or mixed relative to baselines: on Sintel (Tab. 2) the method trails π³ on several metrics; in Tab. 6, removing ground-truth cameras actually improves PSNR on RealEstate10K and DL3DV, which weakens the narrative that priors uniformly help and deserves more analysis. Gains in Tab. 5 are also modest (~2.5 points average).

Reproducibility is uncertain: code and models are only 'publicly available soon.' Training requires a cluster of 32 H20 GPUs and 15 datasets, and key details (curriculum schedules, data mixing ratios) are deferred to the appendix at a coarse level of specificity.

Fairness of comparisons is a concern: WorldMirror is trained on a large 15-dataset mixture with prior-conditioned augmentation, while some baselines (e.g., VGGT, π³) were not. The paper does not isolate how much of the gain comes from additional data/training versus the proposed architectural contributions. The no-prior WorldMirror results partially mitigate this, but the confound is not explicitly discussed.

Presentation issues: several important details (losses, dynamic prior injection, curriculum learning) are relegated to the appendix with Sec. A.2 referenced before it exists in reading order; Table 2 mixes bold and underlined formatting inconsistently; Fig. 6 axis labels are unreadable at the printed scale. The main text (Sec. 3) is thin for a method paper, with the actual training recipe scattered across the appendix.
Only 5 scenes are evaluated for VR-NeRF, a very small evaluation sample for that benchmark.

strengths: Broad empirical evaluation across many tasks (point map reconstruction, camera pose, depth, surface normals, novel view synthesis) with state-of-the-art or competitive results against recent baselines such as VGGT, π³, FLARE, AnySplat, and StableNormal

The unified 'any-prior' input design (poses, intrinsics, depth) is practically useful, and the dynamic prior-injection scheme plus ablations (Tab. 5, Fig. 6) provide reasonable evidence that priors improve both the targeted task and other tasks

The paper is generally well organized, with training details, losses (Sec. A.1), data composition (Sec. A.2), and an honest limitations section covering weak dynamic/driving scenes and resolution/view-count constraints
Ablations on prior embedding (single token vs. dense Plücker/raymap), 3DGS head design, and post-optimization initialization (Tab. 8) are informative and support several design choices
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the method is essentially VGGT (from which the backbone is initialized) augmented with extra input tokens and additional prediction heads; prior-conditioned reconstruction has already been explored by Pow3R and UniDepth, so the contribution is largely an engineering consolidation rather than a new idea

Attribution of gains is unclear: the model is trained on 15 datasets with 32 H20 GPUs and initialized from pretrained VGGT, yet no experiment isolates how much improvement stems from the proposed prior prompting versus simply more data, compute, and multi-task supervision relative to baselines trained on less data

Comparison fairness is questionable in places: Tab. 2's camera-pose evaluation excludes datasets used in CUT3R training but the authors' own much larger training mixture is not scrutinized equally, and on Sintel the method is actually worse than π³ on ATE (0.074 vs. 0.067) despite the text's 'superior zero-shot performance' framing

Prior prompting itself is technically simple (an MLP-encoded token concatenated, or depth tokens added) and the camera/intrinsics embedding is close to standard practice; the curriculum and pruning ideas are borrowed from VGGT and AnySplat respectively

The camera pose token packs a full pose into a single 7-D vector per view, but there is no analysis of failure modes when pose priors are noisy or partially available in practice, which is the realistic deployment scenario motivating the paper
Code and models are only 'publicly available soon', limiting reproducibility at review time, and several quantitative details (e.g., dataset mixing ratios, view-count sampling) are underspecified

strengths: Addresses a clear and well-motivated gap: existing feed-forward reconstruction models (DUSt3R, VGGT, etc.) only consume raw images and exclude tasks like surface normal estimation and novel view synthesis. The proposed Multi-Modal Prior Prompting mechanism flexibly integrates camera poses, calibrated intrinsics, and depth priors, which is a genuinely useful capability for real-world deployment where such priors are often available.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation across a remarkably broad set of tasks and benchmarks (point map reconstruction on 7-Scenes/NRGBD/DTU, camera pose on RealEstate10K/Sintel/TUM-dynamics, surface normals on ScanNet/NYUv2/iBims-1, NVS on RealEstate10K/DL3DV/VR-NeRF, plus monocular/video depth in the appendix), with consistent state-of-the-art or highly competitive results against both generalist models (VGGT, pi3) and specialized methods (StableNormal, GeoWizard, AnySplat, FLARE).

The dynamic prior injection scheme (randomly toggling priors during training with zeroing of disabled tokens) is a simple, well-motivated mechanism that enables a single model to operate over all 2^3 prior combinations, and the results in Fig. 6 convincingly show that single modalities improve not just their own task but others as well.

Thoughtful ablations: prior embedding design (single token vs. dense Plucker/raymap encodings) is evaluated with both accuracy and parameter overhead, and the NVS ablation (predicted vs. GT cameras, target-view supervision, GS head design) substantiates each design choice.

Honest and specific limitations section (suboptimal performance on dynamic scenes/driving environments due to training data distribution, resolution constraints of 300-700 pixels, inability to scale to thousands of views), and useful additional analyses (post-optimization with predicted geometry as initialization in Tab. 8).
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is somewhat incremental: the backbone is initialized from pretrained VGGT weights, dense heads reuse DPT, and the 3DGS prediction follows AnySplat's pixel-wise Gaussians with voxelization-based pruning. The core contribution is the prior-token integration and training recipe rather than a new modeling paradigm, which may limit its conceptual impact for a main-track audience.

The claim of being 'the first systematic exploration of multi-modal geometric prior injection within dense multi-view reconstruction frameworks' slightly overstates novelty; Pow3R already incorporates extrinsics/intrinsics/depth as inputs to a DUSt3R-style model, and the distinction (dense regression vs. sparse '3R' paradigms) deserves more careful justification.

Comparisons where WorldMirror uses priors (e.g., 'w/ intrinsics/depth/camera pose' rows in Tab. 1) are not directly matched by prior-conditioned baselines, since no baseline supports priors; this is understandable but means the headline gains partly conflate the conditioning mechanism with the model's stronger backbone/data. A controlled comparison isolating the benefit of priors versus simply a better base model would strengthen the evidence.

Reproducibility is a concern: training uses 32 H20 GPUs over a 15-dataset mixture, code is only promised to be 'publicly available soon', and several important details (exact dataset proportions in each curriculum phase, how pseudo-normals are generated via plane fitting, full evaluation protocols) are relegated or omitted. The compute scale makes independent replication difficult.

Presentation has minor issues: key methodological details (loss definitions, curriculum learning, dynamic prior injection) are deferred entirely to the appendix, some tables mix configurations in ways that complicate direct reading, and there are occasional dangling references (e.g., 'Table 7' cited before its appendix definition in a way that disrupts flow).

Dataset diversity analysis is thin regarding data provenance and licensing for 15 mixed real/synthetic datasets, and the paper does not discuss potential societal considerations for a model that reconstructs scenes from casual photos (privacy of reconstructed indoor environments), though the risk is arguably modest for this research context.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and practical gap: existing feed-forward 3D models are either prior-conditioned but narrow (Pow3R) or multi-task but image-only (VGGT, π3). The unified treatment of flexible prior injection together with comprehensive multi-task prediction (points, depth, cameras, normals, 3DGS) is a useful and well-motivated contribution.

Empirical evaluation is extensive and convincing: point map reconstruction (7-Scenes, NRGBD, DTU), camera pose (RealEstate10K, Sintel, TUM), surface normals (ScanNet, NYUv2, iBims-1), monocular/video depth, and a multi-resolution NVS benchmark, plus comparisons against prior-guided methods (Pow3R, MapAnything) under matched prior conditions.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough: prior embedding strategies (single token vs. dense Plücker/raymap), depth injection (addition vs. concatenation) with FLOPs/time, depth normalization, decoupled vs. joint training, prior dropout sensitivity, and NVS design choices. The finding that priors universally boost all tasks (Fig. 7, Tab. 1) is an interesting empirical insight.

Robustness analysis with realistic noise injection across all prior modalities (Tab. 12) and a formal dropout-probability sweep strengthen the credibility of the 'any-prior' claim beyond clean synthetic settings.

Reproducibility is well supported: full training losses, loss weights, training data list, GPU count, wall-clock training time, memory footprints, and inference latency comparisons are provided; code and weights are promised to be public.

The limitations section is honest and specific (weakness on dynamic/driving scenes, resolution and view-count limits), and an impact statement addressing privacy/misrepresentation concerns is included.
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate. The core mechanism—concatenating prior tokens with image tokens and adding dense depth tokens—is a straightforward combination of ideas already present in Pow3R, MapAnything, OmniVGGT, and VGGT. The strongest claim to novelty is the system unification and the 'universal prior gains' observation, which is empirical rather than a new methodological principle.

The model is initialized from pretrained VGGT weights and trained on 15 datasets; the authors themselves acknowledge that some NVS gains likely stem from broader training data scale. This makes it harder to disentangle architectural contribution from data/compute advantages, and a no-prior WorldMirror vs. π3 comparison (Tab. 2 on Sintel, Tab. 7 on Sintel/KITTI monocular) shows mixed or weaker results in some settings, slightly tempering the blanket 'state-of-the-art' framing.

Evaluation contamination risk is not fully discussed: surface normal evaluation is on ScanNet while ScanNet++ is in the training set, and several evaluation datasets come from distributions closely related to training corpora (e.g., RealEstate10K-style scenes). A clearer statement on train/test overlap is needed.

Some comparisons have resolution or protocol differences (e.g., Tab. 4 DepthSplat at 448×256 vs. WorldMirror at 448×252; Tab. 11 NoPoSplat at 256×256 with center-crop adaptation), which are handled but add caveats to head-to-head conclusions.

The GS head relies on ground-truth camera parameters during rendering supervision, so the pose-free NVS capability is somewhat indirect; a stronger end-to-end analysis of error propagation from predicted cameras into 3DGS would help.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing feed-forward 3D models either accept flexible geometric priors (Pow3R, MapAnything) or predict comprehensive outputs (VGGT), but not both. The unified multi-task + any-prior design is a useful and sensible system contribution.

Evaluation breadth is impressive: point map reconstruction, camera pose, monocular/video depth, surface normals, and novel view synthesis across many benchmarks, plus prior-guided comparisons (Fig. 5) against Pow3R and MapAnything.

The ablation studies are unusually thorough: prior embedding strategy (Tab. 5), prior dropout sensitivity (Tab. 14), noisy-prior robustness (Tab. 12), depth injection and normalization choices (Tabs. 15-16), and decoupled vs. joint training (Tab. 13). These support the main design decisions.

Reproducibility treatment is above average: full loss definitions, loss weights, training data list, wall-clock training time, GPU memory tables, and inference speed comparisons (Tabs. 17-19), plus a statement that code and weights will be released.
An honest limitations section (Appendix G) identifies weaknesses on dynamic/autonomous-driving scenes and view-count/resolution constraints rather than hiding them.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The backbone, geometry heads, and losses are explicitly inherited from VGGT; prior conditioning via token concatenation/single tokens is close to Pow3R and MapAnything; the 3DGS head and voxel pruning follow AnySplat. The core contributions (token merging, dropout of priors, curriculum/decoupled training) are straightforward engineering choices rather than new insights, and the claimed 'emergent synergy' is asserted more than mechanistically explained.

Comparison fairness is confounded by scale. The model is fine-tuned from VGGT's pretrained weights on an aggregate of 15 datasets using 32 H20 GPUs. Many baselines were trained on substantially different (often smaller) data. The paper itself concedes in Sec. 5.4 that NVS gains 'likely stem from... broader training data scale,' which undermines the attribution of SOTA gaps to the architecture.

Train/test separation is ambiguous and potentially problematic. DL3DV is in the training data while DL3DV NVS is a headline benchmark (Tab. 4, Tab. 9); RealEstate10K is described as excluded for pose evaluation (Tab. 2) but the text elsewhere says the model is 'not trained specifically on RealEstate10K for the two-view setting,' leaving its role in NVS training unclear. Exclusion of 7-Scenes, NRGBD, and DTU from training is never explicitly stated. The very large RealEstate10K NVS margins (25.14 vs. 19.96 PSNR) are hard to interpret without clarity here.

SOTA claims are overstated. On Sintel pose, WorldMirror is worse than pi3 on ATE/RPE-trans (Tab. 2); on KITTI and Sintel monocular depth it trails pi3 (Tab. 7). The abstract's 'state-of-the-art performance across diverse benchmarks' does not hold uniformly, and per-benchmark caveats are relegated to the appendix.

Several ablation gains are marginal or mixed. In Tab. 6, 'w/o GS DPT' beats the full model on several metrics (e.g., VR-NeRF LPIPS 0.191 vs. 0.198; SSIM 0.798 vs. 0.811 is small), and in Tab. 5 the 'Single Token' design loses to dense raymaps on focal accuracy (84.43 vs. 86.48) and depth (36.29 vs. 37.40 for intrinsics), weakening the claim that compact tokens are uniformly superior.

The normal head is trained on pseudo-normals derived from ground-truth depth; the paper does not clarify whether sources of these pseudo-labels overlap with the normal evaluation datasets (ScanNet/NYUv2), which could inflate Tab. 3 results relative to specialists trained without such supervision.

Depth priors are added element-wise to image tokens, and the justification is largely cost-based; the interaction between this fusion and the model's reliance on VGGT initialization is not analyzed, so the relative contribution of the new components versus inherited VGGT capability remains partially unclear.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine gap: existing feed-forward 3D reconstruction models are either image-only with multi-task outputs (VGGT, π³) or prior-conditioned with narrow outputs (Pow3R). WorldMirror unifies both flexible prior conditioning and comprehensive multi-task prediction (point maps, depth, normals, cameras, 3D Gaussians) in a single feed-forward model, which is a useful and practical contribution.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this line of work: five task areas (point map reconstruction, camera pose, normals, depth, NVS) across many benchmarks, comparisons against prior-guided methods (Pow3R, MapAnything), plus extensive ablations covering prior embedding strategies (Tab. 5), decoupled vs. joint training (Tab. 13), prior dropout sensitivity (Tab. 14), noise robustness (Tab. 12), depth injection design (Tabs. 15-16), and practical costs (memory, max views, wall-clock training time, inference latency in F and Tab. 19).

The core finding that prior injection yields universal gains across all output tasks (Figs. 5, 7; Tab. 1) is an interesting and well-supported empirical result supporting the claim that input flexibility and multi-task prediction are mutually reinforcing.

The key design decisions are well motivated and ablated: single-token priors outperform dense Plücker/raymap embeddings (Tab. 5), additive depth fusion beats concatenation on both accuracy and cost (Tab. 15), and dual rendering supervision plus independent GS-head positions improve NVS (Tab. 6).

Strong reproducibility posture: code and weights promised public, detailed training hyperparameters, loss formulations (Eqs. 4-9), dataset list, hardware, and wall-clock training time disclosed. The limitations section (App. G) honestly identifies weaknesses in dynamic/autonomous-driving scenes, resolution range, and view-count scaling.
Efficiency claims are backed: prior injection adds negligible latency over VGGT (Tab. 19), and the full 5-task model has only ~13% overhead at 64 views.
weaknesses: Architectural novelty is incremental. The backbone, decoders, and camera/point/depth heads are directly inherited from VGGT (initialized from VGGT pretrained weights), and the new components are fairly simple: MLP-projected single tokens for poses/intrinsics, additive depth tokens, DPT normal/GS heads. The competing prior-guided models (MapAnything, OmniVGGT) are concurrent but conceptually similar; differentiation rests mainly on design choices and results rather than a fundamentally new idea.

The gains partly stem from advantages not isolated by ablation: initialization from VGGT, the 15-dataset training mix (acknowledged as a data advantage for NVS), and heavy compute (32 H20 GPUs). While the paper acknowledges the data advantage, there is no ablation quantifying how much of the improvement over VGGT/π³ comes from pretraining vs. the multi-task/prior design itself.

State-of-the-art claims are overstated in places. WorldMirror is not uniformly best: it trails π³ on Sintel ATE (Tab. 2), monocular Sintel AbsRel, and KITTI depth (Tab. 7); it is second-best on some normal metrics (Tab. 3). The comparison with MapAnything is limited to a bar chart (Fig. 5) with averaged metrics rather than per-benchmark tables, making the head-to-head evidence thin.

Some methodological details are unclear or inconsistent: Eq. (2) indicates the normal head consumes only image tokens (T_img) despite the multi-task framing; the relationship between the curriculum-learning description ('training geometry tasks first, then GS head') in Sec. 2/3 and the two-phase schedule in A.2 could be more precise; minor typos ('Sec. Sec. 3.2', an abstract reference to Fig. 6 before it appears).

3DGS rendering supervision uses ground-truth cameras during training while the model also predicts cameras; the interaction between predicted-camera inference and rendering quality is examined in Tab. 6 ('w/o GT Cameras') but the conclusion about robustness to camera error in real deployments could be deeper.

The claim that WorldMirror is 'the first framework to unify flexible 3D inputs with comprehensive multi-task prediction' should be softened given MapAnything and OmniVGGT; the related-work paragraph does position against them, but the headline claim in Fig. 2 and contributions list reads stronger than the evidence.
